title: Hubble and Chandra composite of ESO 137-001
caption: The galaxy ESO 137-001, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory
celestial: ESO 137-001 · constellation Triangulum Australe · about 200 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Electric blue streaks pour out of the galaxy ESO 137-001 in this image, and a giant stream of gas stretches toward the bottom of the frame. Hubble observations are combined with X-ray data from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory.

The blue streaks are the signature of ram pressure stripping. As a galaxy moves through the hot, thin gas between galaxies in a cluster, that gas pushes against it like a headwind, and the galaxy's own gas is blown out behind it.

The large stream toward the bottom of the frame can only be seen in X-rays. It is gas that has been heated to very high temperatures, glowing at wavelengths no ordinary camera can capture. By pairing Hubble's view with Chandra's, astronomers can trace both the visible streaks and the much hotter gas that the galaxy is losing.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.28 x 3.26 arcminutes) and distance (200 million light years), the frame spans roughly 191,000 × 190,000 light-years. Its light set out about 200 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite pairs visible and near-infrared images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each dataset.
understand.eye: X-rays are invisible to the eye, so the giant gas stream would not be visible at all without Chandra.
